vulnerability.name: CVE-2023-35887
vulnerability.description:
Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor vulnerability in Apache Software Foundation Apache MINA.

In SFTP servers implemented using Apache MINA SSHD that use a RootedFileSystem, logged users may be able to discover "exists/does not exist" information about items outside the rooted tree via paths including parent navigation ("..") beyond the root, or involving symlinks.

This issue affects Apache MINA: from 1.0 before 2.10. Users are recommended to upgrade to 2.10

statements.status_notes: This information-disclosure issue affects only SFTP servers built with Apache MINA SSHD that use a RootedFileSystem. The bundled MINA SSHD 2.9.2 ships only inside the scanner engine that runs on the analysis machine, and only its common and core modules are present: RootedFileSystem (part of sshd-common) is bundled, but the SFTP module (org.apache.sshd:sshd-sftp) that contains the SFTP server is not. In the scanner engine MINA SSHD serves only as an optional SSH client backend for Subversion svn+ssh:// connections, no SSH or SFTP server is ever created, and no code outside MINA SSHD uses RootedFileSystem, so it never serves files to anyone. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2025-7962
vulnerability.description: In Jakarta Mail versions prior to 2.0.2 it is possible to perform an SMTP Injection by utilizing the \r and \n UTF-8 characters to separate different messages.

statements.status_notes: This issue is SMTP injection in Jakarta Mail before 2.0.2: carriage-return or line-feed characters can end one SMTP command and start another, so it needs attacker-controlled text containing those characters to reach the library's SMTP commands. SonarQube sends every e-mail through Apache Commons Email, which parses each address with Jakarta Mail and rejects any address that contains a carriage return or line feed, including quoted forms. The sender address and SMTP server settings can only be set by an administrator. The older Jakarta Mail 1.6.8 jar in Elasticsearch's security module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) is a separate copy that SonarQube never uses to send mail. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-56745
vulnerability.description: Netty is a network application framework for development of protocol servers and clients. In versions 4.2.0.Final through 4.2.15.Final and 4.1.0.Final through 4.1.135.Final, the `SpdyHttpDecoder` handler in Netty's SPDY-to-HTTP codec allocates a pooled `ByteBuf` when processing a client-initiated `SYN_STREAM` frame with `FLAG_FIN=0` and stores the partially constructed `FullHttpRequest` in `messageMap`; when the remote peer sends `RST_STREAM` for that stream or the accumulated content exceeds `maxContentLength`, the decoder removes the entry but does not release the pooled `ByteBuf`, causing native memory exhaustion. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec-http's SpdyHttpDecoder does not release a pooled buffer for a partially received SPDY stream that is reset or exceeds its content limit, a memory-exhaustion denial of service through the SPDY-to-HTTP codec. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts as a separate process: the HTTP server modules (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) and the AI inference module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. No class in any bundled Elasticsearch module outside Netty itself references Netty's SPDY package: the HTTP server modules decode HTTP/1.1 only, and the inference module uses Netty only as an outbound HTTP client. The SPDY codec is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-55831
vulnerability.description: Netty is a network application framework for development of protocol servers and clients. Prior to 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, Netty's SPDY SETTINGS decoder accepts a peer-declared SETTINGS entry count up to the 24-bit frame-length limit and materializes every unique setting ID in `DefaultSpdySettingsFrame`, allowing a remote SPDY/3.1 peer to send a syntactically valid roughly 2 MiB SETTINGS frame that creates 262144 map entries and amplifies network input into heap growth and ordered-map insertion work. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-55833
vulnerability.description: Netty is a network application framework for development of protocol servers and clients. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-56819
vulnerability.description: Netty is a network application framework for development of protocol servers and clients. In versions 4.2.0.Final through 4.2.15.Final and 4.1.0.Final through 4.1.135.Final, a remote unauthenticated peer can leak one direct `ByteBuf` per HTTP/2 `DATA` frame in applications that enable HTTP/2 content decompression via `DelegatingDecompressorFrameListener`. When a `DATA` frame is processed for a stream whose decompressor has already been closed, `Http2Decompressor.decompress(...)` calls `decompressor.writeInbound(data.retain())` and does not release the retained buffer on the error path, eventually exhausting direct memory and crashing the JVM. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec-http2 can leak one direct buffer per HTTP/2 DATA frame in applications that enable HTTP/2 content decompression through DelegatingDecompressorFrameListener. This copy is in the AI inference module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. No class in any bundled Elasticsearch module outside Netty itself references DelegatingDecompressorFrameListener, so HTTP/2 content decompression is never enabled and the leaking path never runs. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-68497
vulnerability.description: jackson-databind binds a JSON string to a javax.xml.datatype.Duration or javax.xml.datatype.XMLGregorianCalendar field by passing the raw string verbatim to DatatypeFactory.newDuration(value) or newXMLGregorianCalendar(value) in CoreXMLDeserializers.Std._deserialize. These deserializers are registered by default with no opt-in, so a plain ObjectMapper or JsonMapper with no polymorphic typing and no special configuration reaches this path. The XML Schema lexical grammar permits numeric components of arbitrary length, which the JDK materializes through the native BigInteger(String) and BigDecimal(String) constructors, both quadratic in digit count. Because the digits sit inside a JSON string token rather than a JSON number token, jackson-core's StreamReadConstraints.maxNumberLength guard never applies; jackson's own NumberDeserializers call validateIntegerLength or validateFPLength before parsing a stringified number, but the XML datatype deserializer omits that pre-check. An unauthenticated attacker can therefore submit a single request of a few megabytes, such as a Duration value consisting of the letter P followed by several million digits and the letter Y, and force tens of seconds to several minutes of single-threaded CPU work; a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a server's worker threads. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.0.0 before 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 before 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 before 2.22.2, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 before 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 before 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.10, 2.21.6, 2.22.2, 3.1.6, or 3.2.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-68497 is a CPU-exhaustion flaw in jackson-databind's CoreXMLDeserializers: a JSON string bound to a property of type javax.xml.datatype.Duration or javax.xml.datatype.XMLGregorianCalendar is parsed with very expensive BigInteger and BigDecimal arithmetic. Exploitation requires deserializing attacker-controlled JSON into a type that declares such a property. This copy (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/jackson-databind-2.18.9.jar, loaded by the Elasticsearch search process) is used only by the Azure SDK and the Microsoft authentication library inside Elasticsearch's AI inference module. Elasticsearch calls them for one purpose: to obtain an access token from Microsoft Entra ID for an Azure OpenAI inference endpoint configured with Entra ID client-credential authentication. The token client is built with the tenant, client and scope settings only and no custom authority, so the JSON it parses is the token response returned by Microsoft Entra ID over TLS, never content supplied by an attacker. Neither library references javax.xml.datatype at all, so no model bound by this copy has a Duration or XMLGregorianCalendar property, and neither enables default typing. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-89407
vulnerability.description:
NumberInput.looksLikeValidNumber() in FasterXML jackson-core pre-validates "stringified numbers" with two regular expressions: PATTERN_FLOAT ([+-]?[0-9]*[\.]?[0-9]+([eE][+-]?[0-9]+)?), present since 2.17.0, and PATTERN_FLOAT_TRAILING_DOT, added in 2.17.2. PATTERN_FLOAT places adjacent quantifiers over the same character class -- an optional [0-9]* run, an optional dot, then a required [0-9]+ run -- so input that ultimately fails to match forces Java's backtracking engine to retry every possible split point of the digit run. 



Matching cost therefore grows with the square of the input length. 



An attacker who can supply JSON that an application deserializes into a numeric target type reaches this method through jackson-databind's default String-to-number coercion (StdDeserializer and NumberDeserializers for BigDecimal, BigInteger, Double and Float). 



Because StreamReadConstraints.maxStringLength defaults to 20,000,000 characters, no constraint bounds the input before it reaches the regex. 



Testing by the reporter confirmed O(n^2) growth across five consecutive input-size doublings, with a single 160,000-character string consuming roughly 74 seconds in one call; a small number of concurrent requests of ordinary body size can therefore exhaust a server's request-handling thread pool. 



The affected method does not exist before 2.17.0, so 2.16.x and earlier releases are not affected. 



The fix replaces both regular expressions with a hand-rolled single-pass scan.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2024-41909
vulnerability.description:
Like many other SSH implementations, Apache MINA SSHD suffered from the issue that is more widely known as CVE-2023-48795. An attacker that can intercept traffic between client and server could drop certain packets from the stream, potentially causing client and server to consequently end up with a connection for which 
some security features have been downgraded or disabled, aka a Terrapin 
attack

The mitigations to prevent this type of attack were implemented in Apache MINA SSHD 2.12.0, both client and server side. Users are recommended to upgrade to at least this version. Note that both the client and the server implementation must have mitigations applied against this issue, otherwise the connection may still be affected.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2024-41909 is Apache MINA SSHD's instance of the Terrapin SSH handshake weakness (CVE-2023-48795): an attacker who can intercept and modify traffic between an SSH client and server can drop handshake messages and silently downgrade some connection security features when ChaCha20-Poly1305 or CBC with encrypt-then-MAC is negotiated. The fix is strict key exchange, which both the SSH client and the SSH server must support; MINA SSHD adds it in 2.12.0. The bundled MINA SSHD 2.9.2 is not part of the SonarQube server runtime; it ships only in the scanner engine that runs on the analysis machine, where it serves solely as an optional SSH client backend for Subversion SCM operations (blame and changed-file detection) over svn+ssh:// and is used only when the scanner JVM is started with -Dsvnkit.ssh.client=apache. When that option is used, exploitation still requires an active man-in-the-middle position between the analysis machine and the customer's Subversion server, so the risk is reduced but not eliminated.
statements.action_statement: Apache MINA SSHD versions before 2.12.0 are affected (2.12.0 adds strict key exchange on the client side). SonarQube Community Build 26.11 bundles 2.9.2 inside the scanner engine. Releases from 2026.4 onward bundle 2.9.2, while the 2026.1 LTA bundles 2.16.0. Customers using svn+ssh:// with -Dsvnkit.ssh.client=apache can mitigate by disabling chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com and either the CBC ciphers or the -etm@openssh.com MACs on their Subversion SSH server (connections continue to work, since the client also offers AES-CTR and AES-GCM), or by using an HTTPS Subversion URL. Customers not analyzing Subversion projects over svn+ssh:// with that option are not using this component.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-89425
vulnerability.description: UTF8DataInputJsonParser._reportInvalidToken() in FasterXML jackson-core builds the offending-token text for its error message by appending Java identifier characters to a StringBuilder in a loop that has no upper bound. Unlike the three sibling parser implementations, including UTF8StreamJsonParser, it never consults ErrorReportConfiguration.getMaxErrorTokenLength() (default 256). A malformed token supplied to a parser created through JsonFactory.createParser(DataInput) is therefore accumulated in full. No StreamReadConstraints setting mitigates this: maxDocumentLength cannot be applied to DataInput sources at all, and maxStringLength does not cover this path because the accumulation bypasses ReadConstrainedTextBuffer. The reporter measured a 20,000,109-character exception message from a 20-million-character malformed token on the DataInput path, against 367 characters for identical input on the InputStream path. Scaling the payload drives the StringBuilder, which also incurs byte-to-char expansion and internal array doubling, to many times the raw payload size and can trigger OutOfMemoryError for the whole JVM. UTF8DataInputJsonParser was introduced in 2.8.0 together with createParser(DataInput); releases before 2.8.0 do not contain the affected class.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-83557
vulnerability.description: DefaultBaseTypeLimitingValidator is the PolymorphicTypeValidator applied automatically whenever @JsonTypeInfo is used without an explicitly configured custom validator. It denies polymorphic resolution only for a fixed set of "unsafe base types", and its isSafeSubType method returns true unconditionally for every base type outside that set. java.lang.Comparable was absent from the list despite being implemented by a very large fraction of JDK and application classes, comparable in breadth to java.io.Serializable, which is on the list for that reason. An application declaring an @JsonTypeInfo-annotated property or class with Comparable as its base type, and no custom PolymorphicTypeValidator, will accept a type identifier for essentially any class implementing Comparable. This yields an attacker-controlled object instantiation primitive; a demonstrated case constructs a java.io.File for an arbitrary attacker-chosen path, which becomes path-traversal-adjacent if the application subsequently calls path-sensitive methods on the value. No class implementing Comparable has been identified that yields code execution through deserialization alone. Global Default Typing via activateDefaultTyping is not affected, because that method structurally requires an explicit PolymorphicTypeValidator argument. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.11.0 before 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 before 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 before 2.22.2, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 before 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 before 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.10, 2.21.6, 2.22.2, 3.1.6, or 3.2.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-83557 is a gap in jackson-databind's DefaultBaseTypeLimitingValidator: java.lang.Comparable is missing from its deny list of unsafe base types, so a @JsonTypeInfo polymorphic property whose base type is Comparable accepts a class name for almost any Comparable class. Exploitation requires such a Comparable-based polymorphic declaration on a model that receives attacker-controlled JSON. This copy (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/jackson-databind-2.18.9.jar, loaded by the Elasticsearch search process) is used only by the Azure SDK and the Microsoft authentication library inside Elasticsearch's AI inference module. Elasticsearch calls them for one purpose: to obtain an access token from Microsoft Entra ID for an Azure OpenAI inference endpoint configured with Entra ID client-credential authentication. The token client is built with the tenant, client and scope settings only and no custom authority, so the JSON it parses is the token response returned by Microsoft Entra ID over TLS, never content supplied by an attacker. Neither library declares a polymorphic model with a Comparable base type (the Azure SDK's only @JsonTypeInfo reference is in a helper that reads annotations), and neither enables default typing. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59901
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, the `Bzip2Decoder` handler in Netty's compression codec pipeline is vulnerable to a denial-of-service attack through a malformed bzip2 stream that permanently captures the event-loop thread in an infinite loop. The vulnerability exists in the run-length encoding (RLE) state machine within [`Bzip2BlockDecompressor.read()`]. This issue has been fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec's Bzip2Decoder can enter an infinite loop on a malformed bzip2 stream, capturing the event-loop thread. Exploitation requires an application that passes attacker-controlled data through Netty's bzip2 decoder. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4, elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference). No class in any bundled Elasticsearch module outside Netty itself references Netty's bzip2 codec, so the decoder is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-91776
vulnerability.description: TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer() in FasterXML jackson-databind caches the resolved deserializer under the raw, attacker-supplied type ID. When name-based polymorphism is configured with a fallback, for example @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.NAME, defaultImpl = ...), every distinct unrecognized type ID resolves to the same fallback deserializer but is retained as its own key in the _deserializers map. That map has no configurable bound and lives for the lifetime of the type deserializer, so an attacker who can repeatedly supply fresh unknown type IDs causes monotonic memory retention across requests. The reporter observed 10,000 retained entries from 10,000 distinct unknown IDs, against a single entry for a control that repeated one unknown ID the same number of times, isolating attacker-controlled key cardinality from request volume. Exploitation requires an application that enables name-based polymorphism with a defaultImpl or equivalent fallback, accepts attacker-influenced type IDs, and reuses a long-lived ObjectMapper across requests. The fix stops caching fallback resolutions for unrecognized IDs and bounds both the number of cached entries and the length of a cacheable type ID.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-91776 is unbounded cache growth in jackson-databind's TypeDeserializerBase._findDeserializer(), which requires name-based polymorphism with a fallback type or a DeserializationProblemHandler that resolves unknown type ids, plus attacker-supplied type ids. This copy (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/jackson-databind-2.18.9.jar, loaded by the Elasticsearch search process) is used only by the Azure SDK and the Microsoft authentication library inside Elasticsearch's AI inference module. Elasticsearch calls them for one purpose: to obtain an access token from Microsoft Entra ID for an Azure OpenAI inference endpoint configured with Entra ID client-credential authentication. The token client is built with the tenant, client and scope settings only and no custom authority, so the JSON it parses is the token response returned by Microsoft Entra ID over TLS, never content supplied by an attacker. Neither library declares such a polymorphic model, registers a DeserializationProblemHandler or enables default typing. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-91777
vulnerability.description: Forward-reference completion for @JsonIdentityInfo object IDs in FasterXML jackson-databind performs a linear scan of the pending-reference accumulator for every resolved ID. The affected paths are CollectionDeserializer.CollectionReferringAccumulator.resolveForwardReference() and the equivalent implementation in MapDeserializer. When a document first creates N unresolved object-ID references in an identity-enabled collection or map and then defines those same IDs in reverse order, completion performs on the order of N * (N + 1) / 2 identity comparisons, so a shallow document whose size grows linearly causes quadratic CPU work during deserialization. The reporter instrumented equals() calls on the ID class and measured exactly 2,003,000 comparisons at N = 2,000, against zero comparisons in the pending-reference lookup path for an equally sized control in which every reference was already resolved. The input requires no deep nesting and no syntactically unusual JSON. Exploitation requires an application that deserializes attacker-influenced JSON into an identity-enabled collection or map. The fix replaces the repeated linear lookup with a keyed pending-reference structure.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-91777 is quadratic CPU use in jackson-databind's forward-reference resolution for object identities, which requires deserializing attacker-influenced JSON into a collection or map of a type annotated with @JsonIdentityInfo. This copy (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/jackson-databind-2.18.9.jar, loaded by the Elasticsearch search process) is used only by the Azure SDK and the Microsoft authentication library inside Elasticsearch's AI inference module. Elasticsearch calls them for one purpose: to obtain an access token from Microsoft Entra ID for an Azure OpenAI inference endpoint configured with Entra ID client-credential authentication. The token client is built with the tenant, client and scope settings only and no custom authority, so the JSON it parses is the token response returned by Microsoft Entra ID over TLS, never content supplied by an attacker. Neither library has a type annotated with @JsonIdentityInfo, so the identity resolution path is never used. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59899
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, `HttpContentEncoder` (the superclass of the production handler `HttpContentCompressor`) maintains a per-channel `ArrayDeque<CharSequence>` named `acceptEncodingQueue` that accumulates attacker-controlled data without any size limit. The queue is filled on the I/O thread for every inbound HTTP request and drained only when the application later writes a non-1xx response. This creates a resource exhaustion vulnerability when an attacker exploits HTTP/1.1 pipelining to flood the connection with requests faster than the application produces responses. This issue has been fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-59899 is a memory-exhaustion denial of service in Netty's HttpContentCompressor: a client that pipelines HTTP/1.1 requests on one connection faster than responses are returned makes a per-connection queue grow without limit. These copies are in the HTTP server modules of the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security), and Elasticsearch's HTTP listener does use this compressor. Exploitation requires a client that can open a connection to the search engine's HTTP port (sonar.search.port, default 9001) and pipeline HTTP/1.1 requests on it. SonarQube binds that port to the host's loopback address by default (sonar.search.host), Elasticsearch there has no authentication and it permits cross-origin browser requests, so a web page opened in a browser on the SonarQube host, or any process on that host, can do this. The impact is limited to slowing or stopping the search process, so the risk is reduced but not eliminated.
statements.action_statement: SonarQube Community Build 26.11.0.134175 bundles Elasticsearch 9.4.7 with Netty 4.1.135.Final, which is affected (Netty versions before 4.1.136.Final). Keep sonar.search.host at its default loopback address and do not expose the search port (sonar.search.port, default 9001) beyond the SonarQube host. Elasticsearch on the SonarQube host cannot be firewalled from a browser or process on that host, so this reduces but does not remove the exposure.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-49844
vulnerability.description:
Improper encoding of non-finite floating-point values during MapMessage JSON serialization in Apache Log4j API produces output that is not valid JSON. This issue affects Apache Log4j API versions 2.13.1 through 2.25.4 and version 2.26.0.

The fix for CVE-2026-34481 did not cover all code paths: when a MapMessage contains a non-finite IEEE 754 value (NaN, Infinity, or -Infinity), MapMessage.asJson() emits the corresponding bare token. RFC 8259 does not permit these tokens, so a conformant parser rejects the resulting document.

The defect is reachable only when both of the following conditions hold:

  *  The application uses the  message resolver https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/manual/json-template-layout.html#event-template-resolver-message  of JsonTemplateLayout or any other layout that relies on MapMessage.asJson() or MapMessage.getFormattedMessage(new String[]{"JSON"}).
  *  The application logs a MapMessage that contains an attacker-controlled floating-point value.


An attacker who can supply a non-finite value can cause the affected layout to emit malformed JSON, which may corrupt the enclosing log record or disrupt downstream log ingestion and parsing.

Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Log4j API 2.25.5 or 2.26.1, both of which emit RFC 8259-compliant JSON for non-finite values.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-49844 makes Log4j emit invalid JSON when a layout serializes a MapMessage (MapMessage.asJson() or its JSON format) that contains an attacker-controlled non-finite floating-point value. This copy is the private Log4j packaged inside the Elastic APM Java agent in the telemetry module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/apm/elastic-apm-agent-java8-1.55.6.jar). The Elasticsearch launcher attaches the agent to the search process with instrumentation turned off, and the agent's Log4j is isolated from Elasticsearch's own logging. The agent uses it only to write its own diagnostic messages, through either a plain pattern layout or the ECS JSON layout, and no agent class outside Log4j creates a MapMessage. No MapMessage, attacker-controlled or otherwise, is ever serialized by this copy. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-73508
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, io.netty.handler.codec.dns.AbstractDnsRecord, io.netty.handler.codec.dns.DefaultDnsRecordDecoder.decodeRecord(), and io.netty.handler.codec.dns.DnsCodecUtil.decompressDomainName() failed to release retained or newly allocated ByteBuf objects when IDN.toASCII() or encodeDomainName() rejected a malformed domain name, allowing unauthenticated remote DNS packets to leak direct memory incrementally until denial of service. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-73508 is a direct-memory leak in netty-codec-dns's record decoding when a malformed domain name in a DNS response is rejected, reachable only through Netty's asynchronous DNS resolver. This copy is in the AI inference module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference). Elasticsearch's own networking resolves names through the JDK resolver. When an inference endpoint is defined, the module's Netty-based clients (the AWS SDK client used for Amazon Bedrock and SageMaker, and the Azure SDK HTTP client) keep the JDK resolver. Netty's DNS resolver therefore never processes DNS packets. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59171
vulnerability.description: JSON-java is a reference implementation of a JSON package in Java. From version 20150729 through 20260522, JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue can accumulate unbounded numeric tokens before JSONObject.stringToNumber passes them to BigInteger or BigDecimal conversion without a length limit. An application that parses attacker-controlled JSON or XML through JSONObject, JSONArray, or XML.toJSONObject can spend super-linear CPU time converting a sufficiently long numeric literal, blocking request-handling threads and causing denial of service. Strict mode and keep-strings settings in JSONParserConfiguration do not prevent the affected conversion path. Version 20260719 limits numeric conversion length.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-59171 is super-linear CPU use when org.json converts a very long numeric literal while parsing attacker-controlled JSON or XML through JSONObject, JSONArray or XML.toJSONObject. In the SonarQube application jar org.json is used only by the SAML authentication status page, which writes JSON and never parses it, and Hazelcast uses its own separate relocated copy only to read its bundled configuration schema. No attacker-controlled JSON or XML reaches org.json parsing. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-19032
vulnerability.description: jackson-databind's deserializer for java.nio.file.Path resolves an attacker-supplied URI without restricting the URI scheme. In JDKFromStringDeserializer.NioPathHelper.deserialize, a string bound from untrusted JSON is passed to new URI(value) and then to Path.of(uri). When that throws FileSystemNotFoundException, the code enumerates ServiceLoader<FileSystemProvider> and calls provider.getPath(uri) on the first provider whose scheme matches the attacker-chosen scheme. Untrusted JSON can therefore select and drive an arbitrary registered FileSystemProvider during readValue under a default JsonMapper, and forces provider class loading at the same time. With only the JDK built-in providers (file, jar/zipfs) present, the resolved path is inert and no mount or network I/O occurs; further impact requires a side-effecting third-party FileSystemProvider on the classpath. This affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 2.8.0 before 2.18.10, from 2.19.0 before 2.21.6, and from 2.22.0 before 2.22.2, and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind from 3.0.0 before 3.1.6 and from 3.2.0 before 3.2.2. Users should upgrade to 2.18.10, 2.21.6, 2.22.2, 3.1.6, or 3.2.2. Binding java.nio.file.Path from untrusted JSON should be avoided regardless of version.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-19032 concerns jackson-databind's java.nio.file.Path deserializer: when untrusted JSON is bound to a Path-typed property, the attacker-chosen URI scheme selects an installed FileSystemProvider. Exploitation requires deserializing attacker-controlled JSON into a type that declares a Path property, or enabling default typing. This copy (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/jackson-databind-2.18.9.jar, loaded by the Elasticsearch search process) is used only by the Azure SDK and the Microsoft authentication library inside Elasticsearch's AI inference module. Elasticsearch calls them for one purpose: to obtain an access token from Microsoft Entra ID for an Azure OpenAI inference endpoint configured with Entra ID client-credential authentication. The token client is built with the tenant, client and scope settings only and no custom authority, so the JSON it parses is the token response returned by Microsoft Entra ID over TLS, never content supplied by an attacker. The only Path values in these libraries are file locations held by non-Jackson helper classes, no Jackson model declares a Path property, and neither library enables default typing. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-75595
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to 4.1.137.Fina and 4.2.17.Final, io.netty.handler.ssl.SslClientHelloHandler#decode checks the wrong offset before reading the four-byte TLS handshake header, so a ClientHello whose handshake header spans records can cause an IndexOutOfBoundsException and invoke select(ctx, null). This selects the default SslContext instead of the SNI-specific context. In deployments where per-SNI clientAuth=REQUIRE is the sole mutual TLS gate, the default SslContext uses clientAuth=NONE or clientAuth=OPTIONAL, and no application-layer certificate verification exists, an unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the protected route's mutual TLS requirement. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.137.Final and 4.2.17.Final.

statements.status_notes: [sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar; sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar] CVE-2026-75595 is an offset check error in Netty's SslClientHelloHandler: a TLS ClientHello whose handshake header spans records makes SniHandler fall back to the default TLS context instead of the context selected for the requested server name, which can bypass a per-name mutual TLS requirement. These copies are in the HTTP server modules of the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security). Elasticsearch does not use SniHandler. Its HTTP layer has a TLS handshake throttle built on SslClientHelloHandler, and it is added to a connection when TLS is enabled on the Elasticsearch HTTP listener, which a standard Community Build does not configure. With TLS, Elasticsearch applies one fixed TLS context and does not install an SniHandler, so it does not select a context by server name. The fallback this CVE causes therefore has no effect. Not exploitable. [sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar] CVE-2026-75595 is an offset check error in Netty's SslClientHelloHandler: a TLS ClientHello whose handshake header spans records makes SniHandler fall back to the default TLS context instead of the context selected for the requested server name. This copy is in the AI inference module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. SslClientHelloHandler and SniHandler run only on the server side of a TLS connection; the only references to them in this module are in Reactor Netty, in its server support and in its channel metrics handler and SNI provider classes (AbstractChannelMetricsHandler, SniProvider), and the module never starts a Reactor Netty server. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-102554
vulnerability.description: Allocation of resources without limits or throttling (CWE-770) during Java object deserialization in Google Guava versions 4.0 through 33.7.1 allows an attacker to cause a Denial of Service via OutOfMemoryError. When deserializing CompactHashMap, CompactHashSet, or MapMakerInternalMap instances, Guava eagerly allocates an array based on a caller-specified size parameter without throttling, permitting memory exhaustion from crafted serialization streams.

statements.status_notes: This issue affects Java deserialization of certain Guava collection classes, so it needs an ObjectInputStream reading attacker-supplied bytes. In the bundled Elasticsearch search engine no Elasticsearch class creates an ObjectInputStream or reads serialized objects, and the library helpers that could (for example commons-lang3 SerializationUtils, the Google HTTP client data stores and Netty's object decoder) are not called by any Elasticsearch code. Serialized data therefore never reaches these Guava classes. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59921
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, HttpPostRequestEncoder constructs multipart HTTP request bodies by directly concatenating user-supplied filenames and field names into Content-Disposition MIME headers without validating or sanitizing CRLF characters (\r\n). Since MIME headers are delimited by CRLF, an attacker who controls the filename can inject arbitrary MIME headers into the multipart body part. The root cause is that neither the encoder nor the FileUpload implementations' setFilename() methods, which only check for null, neutralize CRLF characters before the filename is embedded into the header. This issue has been fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec-http's HttpPostRequestEncoder builds multipart HTTP request bodies by placing caller-supplied file and field names into MIME headers without CRLF filtering, so a caller that passes attacker-controlled names can inject extra MIME headers. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts as a separate process: the HTTP server modules (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) and the AI inference module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. No Elasticsearch class references this encoder. In the inference module the only reference is Reactor Netty's form-sending client helper, which no class in the module calls; the Azure SDK client sends plain request bodies. The encoder is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59898
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework.  Prior to versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, ab attacker can force WebSocket upgrade via the lax V07 (or V08) handshaker by sending `Sec-WebSocket-Version: 7` and omitting `Connection: Upgrade` / `Upgrade: websocket` headers, completing a protocol switch that a proxy would not recognize as an Upgrade request and enabling HTTP request smuggling / protocol-confusion attacks. This issue has been fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec-http's lax V07/V08 WebSocket server handshaker can be made to switch protocols without the Upgrade headers a proxy would recognize, enabling request smuggling across that proxy. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts as a separate process: the HTTP server modules (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) and the AI inference module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. Elasticsearch's HTTP listener installs no WebSocket handler and no Elasticsearch class references Netty's WebSocket package. In the inference module the only references are in Reactor Netty's server and WebSocket support, and the module never starts a server or opens a WebSocket. The handshaker is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59900
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final, Netty's HTTP/2-to-HTTP/1.x translation layer (`Http2StreamFrameToHttpObjectCodec` and `InboundHttp2ToHttpAdapter`) fails to deduplicate or validate `Host` headers when an HTTP/2 client supplies both the `:authority` pseudo-header and a literal `host` header in a single HEADERS frame. The translator maps `:authority` to `Host` and separately copies the literal `host` header, producing an `HttpRequest` object containing two `Host` headers with attacker-controlled differing values. This issue has been fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: This request-smuggling issue is in Netty's server-side translation of inbound HTTP/2 requests to HTTP/1.x, which can produce a request with two different Host headers. This copy is in the AI inference module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. The module never starts a Reactor Netty server, and Elasticsearch's own HTTP listener does not accept HTTP/2, so no inbound HTTP/2 request is ever translated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-56746
vulnerability.description: Netty is a network application framework for development of protocol servers and clients. Versions 4.2.0.Final through 4.2.15.Final and 4.1.0.Final through 4.1.135.Final, are vulnerable to security control bypass during the origin evaluation process. CorsHandler provides a shortCircuit() configuration designed to reject unauthorized cross-origin requests immediately, acting as a security control before requests reach the application. However, due to a logical operator error in the origin evaluation process, this protection can be entirely bypassed. An attacker can bypass the short-circuit mechanism by sending a request with an Origin: null header. This failure forwards unauthorized requests to the backend application, bypassing intended access controls. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.136.Final and 4.2.16.Final.

statements.status_notes: netty-codec-http's CorsHandler offers a shortCircuit() option meant to reject unauthorized cross-origin requests immediately, but a request with an Origin: null header bypasses that check. Exploitation requires an application that relies on Netty's own CorsHandler for that decision. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts as a separate process: the HTTP server modules (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) and the AI inference module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. Elasticsearch handles cross-origin requests with its own implementation and never uses Netty's CorsHandler: no class in any bundled Elasticsearch module outside Netty itself references Netty's CORS package, and the inference module uses Netty only as an outbound HTTP client. The vulnerable handler is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106452
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.2, net.jpountz.lz4.LZ4BlockInputStream refill() validates that the compressedLen field in a legacy LZ4Block header is nonnegative but allocates a compressed-input buffer of that attacker-controlled size before reading payload data, allowing a header-only stream to request a near-2 GiB allocation and exhaust the JVM heap. Canonical writers emit raw blocks when compression is not smaller than the original block, but vulnerable readers accept non-canonical oversized compressed blocks. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106452 is a heap-exhaustion denial of service in lz4-java's LZ4BlockInputStream, which allocates a buffer sized by an unvalidated compressed-length field from the block header before reading any data. Only the bundled Elasticsearch process loads this copy: the launcher starts Elasticsearch with its own lib directory on the classpath, while SonarQube's web and Compute Engine processes run from the application jar, which carries a newer lz4-java (1.12.0) that is not affected. Elasticsearch never creates an LZ4BlockInputStream: its transport compression decompresses into buffers it sizes itself, by default through Elasticsearch's own forked LZ4 codec. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106450
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.4, net.jpountz.lz4.LZ4FrameInputStream readHeader() allocates two new 4 MiB block buffers whenever a maximum-block-size frame header is read, and the default concatenated-frame mode allows attacker-controlled streams containing many minimal empty frames to trigger roughly 8 MiB of allocation for every 11 input bytes. The stream produces no decompressed output while consuming CPU and garbage-collection time, so decompressed-size limits do not mitigate the issue; readSingleFrame mode is not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.4.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106450 is a CPU and memory amplification flaw in lz4-java's LZ4FrameInputStream, which allocates two buffers of up to 4 MiB for every frame header read from the input. Only the bundled Elasticsearch process loads this copy: the launcher starts Elasticsearch with its own lib directory on the classpath, while SonarQube's web and Compute Engine processes run from the application jar, which carries a newer lz4-java (1.12.0) that is not affected. No class outside lz4-java references LZ4FrameInputStream anywhere in the product, so the vulnerable class is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-75596
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to 4.1.137.Final and 4.2.17.Final, the default io.netty.handler.ssl.SniHandler constructors use the pre-handshake ClientHello aggregation path in handler/src/main/java/io/netty/handler/ssl/SslClientHelloHandler.java at io.netty.handler.ssl.SslClientHelloHandler#decode, where handshakeBuffer.clear() and writeBytes() recopy all previously received body bytes for every additional TLS record. An unauthenticated remote peer can advertise a large ClientHello and deliver its body in thousands of tiny records, causing quadratic CPU work on the event loop before the TLS handshake completes and degrading TLS handling for other clients. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.137.Final and 4.2.17.Final.

statements.status_notes: [sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar; sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar] This denial-of-service issue requires an attacker to deliver a large TLS ClientHello split across many tiny TLS records to a Netty handler that aggregates it before the handshake completes (SslClientHelloHandler, as used by SniHandler). These copies are in the HTTP server modules of the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security). Elasticsearch does not use SniHandler. Its HTTP layer has a TLS handshake throttle built on SslClientHelloHandler, but it is added to a connection only when TLS is enabled on the Elasticsearch HTTP listener, which is not the case in this edition, so the aggregation code never runs. Not exploitable. [sonarqube-26.11.0.134175/elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference/netty-handler-4.1.135.Final.jar] This denial-of-service issue requires an attacker to deliver a large TLS ClientHello split across many tiny TLS records to a Netty handler that aggregates it before the handshake completes (SslClientHelloHandler, as used by SniHandler). This copy is in the AI inference module of the bundled Elasticsearch 9.4.7 (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. These handlers run only on the server side of a TLS connection; the only references to them in this module are in Reactor Netty, in its server support and in its channel metrics handler and SNI provider classes (AbstractChannelMetricsHandler, SniProvider), and the module never starts a Reactor Netty server. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-113730
vulnerability.description: OGNL is an Object Graph Navigation Library for Java. Prior to 3.4.13, the optional stricter-invocation mode in OgnlRuntime.invokeMethod checks the declaring class of the method that OGNL invokes but does not block java.lang.reflect.Method, java.lang.reflect.Constructor, or java.lang.reflect.Field. An attacker-controlled expression can invoke one of these reflection objects as a proxy for a method on a blocked class, causing the real operation to execute inside JDK reflection without passing through the stricter-invocation check again. Exploitation requires an application to evaluate untrusted OGNL expressions, use the default or an equivalently permissive MemberAccess that permits reflection, and rely on stricter invocation as a sandbox. Applications using a restrictive MemberAccess, including Apache Struts with SecurityMemberAccess, are not affected by this bypass. This issue is fixed in 3.4.13.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-113730 is a bypass of OGNL's optional stricter-invocation mode that requires the application to evaluate an attacker-controlled OGNL expression. In SonarQube Community Build 26.11, OGNL is present only as the copy repackaged inside MyBatis 3.5.19 (org.apache.ibatis.ognl) in the application jar loaded by the web server and Compute Engine. The only code that evaluates OGNL is MyBatis's dynamic-SQL engine, which evaluates the test conditions and substitution placeholders written statically in SonarQube's own mapper XML files; every such expression is a fixed name or condition. Request data only supplies the values those fixed expressions are evaluated against, and substituted values are never parsed as expressions. No SonarQube class or bundled plugin builds MyBatis statements from runtime strings or calls OGNL directly. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106453
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.2, LZ4DecompressorWithLength uses getDecompressedLength to trust the four-byte decompressed-length header before validating the compressed input, allowing a five-byte attacker-supplied input whose header declares a large output size to request up to approximately 2 GiB and exhaust the JVM heap. Convenience overloads backed by LZ4FastDecompressor or LZ4SafeDecompressor allocate the untrusted size, while overloads that write to a caller-provided destination buffer are not affected because the caller controls the destination size. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106453 is a heap-exhaustion denial of service in lz4-java's LZ4DecompressorWithLength, which allocates whatever size a four-byte length header in the input declares. Only the bundled Elasticsearch process loads this copy: the launcher starts Elasticsearch with its own lib directory on the classpath, while SonarQube's web and Compute Engine processes run from the application jar, which carries a newer lz4-java (1.12.0) that is not affected. No class outside lz4-java references LZ4DecompressorWithLength anywhere in the product, and Elasticsearch's transport layer passes its own correctly sized output buffer to the block decompressor instead of using the length-header convenience methods. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-59903
vulnerability.description: Netty is an asynchronous, event-driven network application framework. Prior to 4.1.137.Final and 4.2.17.Final, io.netty.handler.codec.http.cors.CorsHandler setVaryHeader replaces application Vary headers such as Authorization or Cookie with Origin, allowing a caching proxy or CDN to reuse authenticated responses across users and disclose sensitive information. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.137.Final and 4.2.17.Final.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-59903 is a cache-poisoning flaw in Netty's CorsHandler.setVaryHeader(), which replaces an existing Vary header such as Vary: Authorization or Vary: Cookie with Vary: Origin, so a caching proxy could reuse an authenticated response for another user. This finding covers the Netty 4.1.135.Final copies bundled with the Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine that SonarQube Community Build 26.11 starts as a separate process: the HTTP server modules (elasticsearch/modules/transport-netty4 and elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-security) and the AI inference module (elasticsearch/modules/x-pack-inference), which uses Netty only for outbound client connections. Elasticsearch handles cross-origin requests with its own implementation and never uses Netty's CorsHandler: no class in any bundled Elasticsearch module outside Netty itself references Netty's CORS package, and the inference module uses Netty only as an outbound HTTP client. The vulnerable method is never invoked. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106449
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.4, net.jpountz.lz4.LZ4BlockInputStream configured with stopOnEmptyBlock set to false handles each well-formed empty LZ4Block by recursively calling refill(), allowing a long sequence of empty blocks in an attacker-controlled compressed stream to exhaust the decoding thread's stack and throw StackOverflowError. The default stopOnEmptyBlock setting is true and is not affected, and the issue does not cause memory corruption. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.4.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106449 is a stack-exhaustion denial of service in lz4-java's LZ4BlockInputStream, reachable only when the stream is created with stopOnEmptyBlock set to false and fed an attacker-controlled run of empty blocks. Only the bundled Elasticsearch process loads this copy: the launcher starts Elasticsearch with its own lib directory on the classpath, while SonarQube's web and Compute Engine processes run from the application jar, which carries a newer lz4-java (1.12.0) that is not affected. Elasticsearch never creates an LZ4BlockInputStream: its transport compression uses only the block decompressor interface, by default through Elasticsearch's own forked LZ4 codec. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106451
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. From 1.7.0 until 1.11.4, net.jpountz.util.Native.load() uses File.createTempFile to create an exclusive temporary .lck file but derives the native-library path by removing the suffix, then FileOutputStream opens that predictable path without exclusive creation, allowing another local user with access to the same shared temporary directory to create or replace the library file before System.load() uses it. Successful exploitation depends on shared-directory permissions, host protections, and winning the race, and can execute native code as the victim; hardened systems may instead cause library loading to fail and fall back to Java implementations. Configurations using a system library, a private java.io.tmpdir, or Java-only implementations are not affected. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.4.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106451 is a local file-replacement race in lz4-java's native library loader, which extracts its bundled native library to a predictable name in the temporary directory before loading it. Only the bundled Elasticsearch process loads this copy: the launcher starts Elasticsearch with its own lib directory on the classpath, while SonarQube's web and Compute Engine processes run from the application jar, which carries a newer lz4-java (1.12.0) that is not affected. Elasticsearch obtains its LZ4 codec only through the pure Java factory or its own forked Java codec, neither of which invokes the native loader, and the Netty LZ4 codecs that would request the native implementation are never instantiated. The native library is never extracted or loaded from this copy. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-77420
vulnerability.description: JLine is a Java library for handling console input. From 3.0.0 until 3.30.15 and 4.3.1, DefaultHistory.matchPatterns(String patterns, String line) in reader/src/main/java/org/jline/reader/impl/history/DefaultHistory.java converts the HISTORY_IGNORE configuration value into a Java regular expression while escaping only part of its syntax, allowing other regex metacharacters to reach the backtracking engine. An attacker who can control application or user configuration can supply a nested-quantifier expression that is reevaluated whenever a command is added to history, consuming excessive CPU and indefinitely blocking the reader thread. vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-110879
vulnerability.description:
jackson-databind validates the outer class of a class-name type ID but accepts attacker-selected classes inside its generic arguments, even when those classes violate the declared type or would be rejected as direct type IDs. This bypasses the generic-argument validation added for CVE-2026-54512 (GHSA-j3rv-43j4-c7qm), of which this is an incomplete fix.



DatabindContext._resolveAndValidateGeneric() checks the outer class against the declared base type and then passes each argument from the type ID to _validateTypeParameter(), which validates the argument against the outer base type rather than enforcing its corresponding declared generic binding. It also invokes validators with arguments that have not passed the subtype check those validators expect. Under the default DefaultBaseTypeLimitingValidator this accepts an unrelated class inside a generic subtype even when the same class is rejected as a direct type ID. Where an allowIfBaseType(...) rule approves the outer type, Jackson substitutes LaissezFaireSubTypeValidator, so the configured validator no longer restricts the embedded arguments. The element type of a plain array type ID such as [Lpkg.Gadget; is likewise left unvalidated once the array's base type is approved.



Affected paths include annotation-based class-name polymorphism with a default Jackson 3.x JsonMapper, configured default typing in both Jackson 2.x and 3.x, and integrations that expose that default typing. The default-validator case requires no application-authored validator: with @JsonTypeInfo(use = Id.CLASS), a direct gadget type ID is rejected as "Not a subtype", while a type ID naming a generic wrapper around the same gadget is accepted and deserialized, including attacker-supplied bean properties. Where class-name default typing permits Map, a property declared as Map<String,String> accepts HashMap<FileSystemXmlApplicationContext,String>; map-key discovery then passes the attacker-controlled JSON property name to the selected class's one-string constructor. With Spring on the classpath and attacker-controlled XML the application can load, that constructor loads the XML and invokes ProcessBuilder.start() under the application account, giving arbitrary command execution.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-77185
vulnerability.description:
Authentication bypass in sshd-core in Apache MINA SSHD versions 2.0.0 to 2.19.0 and 3.0.0-M1 to 3.0.0-M5 for a certain (presumed rare) way to implement an SSH server.




Apache MINA SSHD is a Java library for client- and server-side SSH. In the server part of the library, a mechanism to perform "asynchronous authentication" exists. A server implemented with Apache MINA SSHD must contain explicit code to make use of this feature. The implementation of this feature was flawed and could potentially lead to skipping checking the signature in public-key or hostbased authentication, or returning a wrong result.




Users are recommended to upgrade to Apache MINA SSHD 2.20.0 or 3.0.0-M6, which fix the logic error and which additionally forbid the use of this "asynchronous authentication" mechanism with the public-key or hostbased authentication schemes: if used, the SSH session will be closed and the server will log an entry indicating that asynchronous authentication may be used only with password or keyboard-interactive authentication.

statements.status_notes: This flaw is an authentication bypass in Apache MINA SSHD's server-side asynchronous authentication mechanism, which applies only to an SSH server that explicitly opts into that feature. The bundled Apache MINA SSHD 2.9.2 is not part of the SonarQube server runtime: it ships only inside the scanner engine, which the server provides as a download to scanners, and runs on the analysis machine. There it is used only as an optional SSH client for Subversion svn+ssh:// connections; no code in the scanner engine references the library's SSH server classes, so no SSH server is ever created and the vulnerable server-side code is never executed. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-115290
vulnerability.description: Uncontrolled Recursion (CWE-674) in Elasticsearch can lead to denial of service via Serialized Data with Nested Payloads (CAPEC-230). An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the remote cluster server interface of a node can send a specially crafted request that causes the node to terminate. No credentials are required. The attacker can repeat the request against each reachable node.

statements.status_notes: This flaw is reachable only through the Elasticsearch remote cluster server interface, which serves API key based cross-cluster search and replication and is disabled by default. Its switch, remote_cluster_server.enabled, is a static node setting. Elasticsearch rejects it in a cluster settings update, so a request to the HTTP API cannot open the interface. SonarQube's generated Elasticsearch configuration does not set it. The vulnerable listener is therefore never opened. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-104895
vulnerability.description:
The asynchronous Smile parser (NonBlockingByteArrayParser) uses a raw-binary length prefix taken from untrusted input to allocate a byte[] before the body is read, with no upper bound and no overflow check. On the raw-binary marker 0xFD, _decodeVInt() computes (value << 6) + (i & 0x3F) without the (value >>> 25) != 0 overflow guard present in the blocking SmileParser._readUnsignedVInt, and _startRawBinary then allocates the declared length immediately.



A Smile feed of roughly ten bytes can therefore force an eager allocation of approximately 2 GB, producing an OutOfMemoryError on reactive or asynchronous Smile endpoints. A VInt crafted to overflow int yields a negative length and a NegativeArraySizeException, a RuntimeException that is not a JacksonException and so escapes the parser contract. Either outcome crashes the request or processing thread.



This is the same class of issue as CVE-2020-28491 in the CBOR parser of this library, which was fixed with a LONGEST_NON_CHUNKED_BINARY guard; the asynchronous Smile parser never received the equivalent guard. No privileges or user interaction beyond the ability to submit data for parsing are required.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-104895 is an unbounded allocation in jackson-dataformat-smile's asynchronous (non-blocking) parser, NonBlockingByteArrayParser, which is created only through SmileFactory.createNonBlockingByteArrayParser(). The text and secrets analyzer uses Smile only through the blocking parser, and no class outside Jackson in the plugin creates a non-blocking parser. The asynchronous parser is never instantiated. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-103009
vulnerability.description: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key (CWE-639) in Elasticsearch can lead to Information Disclosure via a specially crafted cross-cluster search request that references an unauthorized shard identifier. Elasticsearch contains an authorization bypass weakness in its handling of cross-cluster search requests made through the Remote Cluster Security (RCS) 2.0 model. An authorization check validates a request against one identifying attribute of the target shard, while a separate, independently-supplied identifying attribute in the same request determines which shard is actually accessed. A holder of a cross-cluster API key authorized for one index can craft a request whose two identifying attributes refer to different indices, causing the request to be authorized against an index they can access while actually operating against a different, unauthorized index. This can expose that index's document contents, field mappings, and other metadata, and in limited cases allows modification of retention-lease state on the unauthorized index.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-103009 lets a caller holding a cross-cluster API key send a crafted cross-cluster search request to an Elasticsearch cluster's remote cluster transport port so that it is authorized against one index but reads another. It only affects clusters that serve cross-cluster search under the API-key-based remote cluster security model with the remote cluster server port enabled, and it is not exploitable through the REST API. The Elasticsearch 9.4.7 search engine bundled in SonarQube Community Build 26.11 has its remote cluster server port disabled, which is Elasticsearch's default. The switch for that port, remote_cluster_server.enabled, is a static node setting. Elasticsearch rejects it in a cluster settings update, so a request to the HTTP API cannot open the port. SonarQube's generated Elasticsearch configuration does not set it. Cross-cluster API keys need Elasticsearch security, and xpack.security.enabled is a static node setting as well. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-68496
vulnerability.description: The Smile parser in FasterXML jackson-dataformats-binary never invokes StreamReadConstraints.validateNameLength() when decoding JSON object property names, so the maxNameLength limit is not enforced for this format. SmileParser._handleLongFieldName() grows its internal name buffer through an unconstrained _growArrayTo() call and performs no length validation. An attacker who can have a Smile document parsed may therefore embed a single property name of unbounded length; the parser buffers the whole name in memory before returning it, whatever maxNameLength is configured to. Because StreamReadConstraints.maxDocumentLength is also disabled by default, nothing else bounds the name under default settings, so the only limits are the attacker's upload capacity and available heap, leading to memory exhaustion and denial of service. No privileges beyond the ability to submit data to a parsing endpoint are required, and exploitation needs only that the bytes reach SmileFactory parsing, directly or through an ObjectMapper configured with the Smile module. jackson-core's own JSON parsers enforce maxNameLength incrementally during name decoding; this gap is specific to the binary formats. maxNameLength and validateNameLength were introduced in jackson-core 2.16.0, so releases before 2.16.0 do not contain the constraint that is left unenforced. This issue is tracked together with the CBOR parser defect in the same vendor advisory, GHSA-3v8f-v6vx-fmrm, which covers both binary formats. The Smile parser defect (jackson-dataformats-binary issue #726) is CVE-2026-68496; the CBOR parser defect (issue #725) is assigned CVE-2026-68495.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-68496 is missing enforcement of the maximum property name length in the Smile parser; Elasticsearch accepts Smile request bodies. These copies are in the bundled Elasticsearch content parsing library (elasticsearch/lib/elasticsearch-x-content-9.4.7.jar). SonarQube starts Elasticsearch with its HTTP port (sonar.search.port, default 9001) bound to the loopback address by default (sonar.search.host) and without authentication on that port, and Elasticsearch accepts cross-origin browser requests from any origin. A process on the SonarQube host can therefore send such a request, and so can a web page open in a browser on that host if the browser allows requests to the loopback address; SonarQube itself never does. The impact is memory or CPU exhaustion of the search process, so the risk is reduced but not eliminated.
statements.action_statement: SonarQube Community Build 26.11.0.134175 bundles Elasticsearch 9.4.7 with jackson-dataformat-smile 2.18.9, which is affected (jackson-dataformat-smile versions before 2.18.10, 2.21.6 and 2.22.2). SonarQube sets Elasticsearch cross-origin access unconditionally and has no setting to turn it off, and a firewall cannot separate the search port from a browser on the SonarQube host, so no configuration removes the exposure. To reduce it, do not browse untrusted web pages from the SonarQube host and keep sonar.search.host at its default loopback address so that other hosts cannot reach the port.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-18036
vulnerability.description: In Bouncy Castle for Java before 1.86, NTRU reduced secret values with the % operator in three helpers whose reference implementations are deliberately division-free, so each reduction was carried out by an integer division whose latency depends on the secret operand. Polynomial.modQ divided by a variable divisor, which a compiler cannot strength-reduce to a multiply the way it can a constant one, so it emitted a division on every call including on the decapsulation path where the dividend derives from the private key; Polynomial.mod3 and NTRUSampling.mod3 divided the secret key polynomials f and g during key generation, the message polynomials r and m during encapsulation, and coefficients recovered during decapsulation. An attacker able to measure that timing can recover information about the NTRU private key. modQ now masks, which is exact because q is always a power of two, and mod3 uses the reference implementation's division-free fold and select; the results are unchanged.

NTRU must be selected explicitly by application code, and no code that can run with this jar on its classpath references the NTRU classes. This jar sits only in the embedded Elasticsearch distribution's certificate-tool directory (elasticsearch/lib/tools/security-cli), which is not on the Elasticsearch server's module path. At each start the Elasticsearch launcher loads this directory only to run its security auto-configuration step, and that step exits before any Bouncy Castle code runs because SonarQube writes xpack.security.autoconfiguration.enabled=false and xpack.security.enabled=false into the Elasticsearch configuration; SonarQube never runs the directory's command line tools (certutil, certgen, reconfigure-node). Not exploitable. vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-71891
vulnerability.description: In Bouncy Castle for Java before 1.86, BLS12_381BasicScheme.keyValidate, and so BLSPublicKeyParameters and every BasicScheme, MessageAugmentation and ProofOfPossession verify and aggregateVerify that gate on it, accepted a public key built on a foreign ECCurve that merely shares BLS12-381's field characteristic. The issue is reachable only where an application constructs an ECPoint on an explicit, non-canonical curve and accepts it as an authority-bearing key; the standard 48-byte compressed-point decoder always supplies the canonical curve and was never affected.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-71889

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-71888
vulnerability.description: In Bouncy Castle for Java before 1.86, the streaming CMS AuthenticatedData parser accepted a message whose digestAlgorithm and authAttrs fields disagreed about whether authenticated attributes were present. RFC 5652 sec. 9.1 pairs the two, requiring that authAttrs be present whenever digestAlgorithm is, and sec. 9.2 makes the MAC cover the DER encoding of authAttrs when they are present and the eContent OCTET STRING directly when they are not. CMSAuthenticatedDataParser has to choose between those two in its constructor, before it can reach authAttrs, which comes later in the SEQUENCE, so it chose on digestAlgorithm alone: for a message with digestAlgorithm absent but authAttrs present it verified the content MAC and then returned the attributes through getAuthAttrs() as though they had been authenticated, when the MAC had never covered them. An attacker able to modify a message in transit could insert an authenticated attribute, such as an RFC 2634 ESSSecurityLabel, into an otherwise valid message while holding neither the key-encryption key nor the content-MAC key, and an application taking an authorization, routing or labelling decision from those attributes would act on attacker-chosen values. The content itself remained MAC-bound. asn1.cms.AuthenticatedData now rejects the mismatched pairing when parsing and CMSAuthenticatedDataParser cross-checks the two fields once authAttrs is read. This is a variant of CVE-2026-59642, which bound the content to the MAC for messages that legitimately carry authAttrs, and which does not address this case. This issue also affects Bouncy Castle for Java LTS before 2.73.13, and Bouncy Castle for Java FIPS (BC-FJA) before bcpkix-fips 1.0.13 (1.0.X series), 2.0.13 (2.0.X series) and 2.1.13 (2.1.X series), and bcutil-fips 2.0.8 (2.0.X series) and 2.1.8 (2.1.X series).

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-68495
vulnerability.description: The CBOR parser in FasterXML jackson-dataformats-binary never invokes StreamReadConstraints.validateNameLength() when decoding JSON object property names, so the maxNameLength limit is not enforced for this format. CBORParser._decodeLongerName() decodes a definite-length property name with no length check, and CBORParser._decodeChunkedName() delegates to the value-oriented _finishChunkedText() routine, which validates maxStringLength rather than maxNameLength. An attacker who can have a CBOR document parsed may therefore embed a single property name of unbounded length; the parser buffers the whole name in memory before returning it, whatever maxNameLength is configured to. Because StreamReadConstraints.maxDocumentLength is also disabled by default, nothing else bounds the name under default settings, so the only limits are the attacker's upload capacity and available heap, leading to memory exhaustion and denial of service. No privileges beyond the ability to submit data to a parsing endpoint are required, and exploitation needs only that the bytes reach CBORFactory parsing, directly or through an ObjectMapper configured with the CBOR module. jackson-core's own JSON parsers enforce maxNameLength incrementally during name decoding; this gap is specific to the binary formats. maxNameLength and validateNameLength were introduced in jackson-core 2.16.0, so releases before 2.16.0 do not contain the constraint that is left unenforced. This issue is tracked together with the Smile parser defect in the same vendor advisory, GHSA-3v8f-v6vx-fmrm, which covers both binary formats. The CBOR parser defect (jackson-dataformats-binary issue #725) is CVE-2026-68495; the Smile parser defect (issue #726) is assigned CVE-2026-68496.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-68495 is missing enforcement of the maximum property name length in the CBOR parser; Elasticsearch accepts CBOR request bodies. These copies are in the bundled Elasticsearch content parsing library (elasticsearch/lib/elasticsearch-x-content-9.4.7.jar). SonarQube starts Elasticsearch with its HTTP port (sonar.search.port, default 9001) bound to the loopback address by default (sonar.search.host) and without authentication on that port, and Elasticsearch accepts cross-origin browser requests from any origin. A process on the SonarQube host can therefore send such a request, and so can a web page open in a browser on that host if the browser allows requests to the loopback address; SonarQube itself never does. The impact is memory or CPU exhaustion of the search process, so the risk is reduced but not eliminated.
statements.action_statement: SonarQube Community Build 26.11.0.134175 bundles Elasticsearch 9.4.7 with jackson-dataformat-cbor 2.18.9, which is affected (jackson-dataformat-cbor versions before 2.18.10, 2.21.6 and 2.22.2). SonarQube sets Elasticsearch cross-origin access unconditionally and has no setting to turn it off, and a firewall cannot separate the search port from a browser on the SonarQube host, so no configuration removes the exposure. To reduce it, do not browse untrusted web pages from the SonarQube host and keep sonar.search.host at its default loopback address so that other hosts cannot reach the port.
