vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-68498
vulnerability.description:
StreamReadConstraints.maxNameLength (default 50,000 characters) is intended to bound how much memory a single JSON Object property name can consume while being parsed, independently of the much larger maxStringLength (default 100,000,000 characters) that bounds ordinary string values. For parsers built over character input - Reader, String or char[] sources, all served by ReaderBasedJsonParser - that bound is not applied while the name is being accumulated. The code path instead re-uses the string-value length check, which is roughly 2000x larger by default.



In the character-input slow path, ReaderBasedJsonParser._parseName2() accumulates the name into the TextBuffer and, when a segment fills, calls TextBuffer.finishCurrentSegment(), which validates only maxStringLength. The correct check, StreamReadConstraints.validateNameLength(int), is reached afterwards in CharsToNameCanonicalizer.findSymbol(), once the entire name has been scanned to its closing quote. By that point the full name - up to maxStringLength characters - has already been buffered in memory.



A remote attacker who can have a single sufficiently long JSON Object property name parsed through this path can force allocation on the order of 100,000,000 characters (approximately 200 MB, with segment bookkeeping pushing real peak usage higher) before any StreamConstraintsException is thrown, instead of the approximately 50,000-character (about 100 KB) bound the API promises. Repeating this across concurrent requests can exhaust the heap and crash the process. No authentication or user interaction is required. Because StreamReadConstraints.maxDocumentLength is disabled by default (-1), nothing else bounds the token first, so the issue is exploitable under default configuration.



Byte-input parsers are not affected: UTF8StreamJsonParser, UTF8DataInputJsonParser and the non-blocking (async) parsers re-validate maxNameLength on every growth of the name-decode buffer via ParserBase._growNameDecodeBuffer(), rejecting an oversized name after allocating only tens of kilobytes. Applications are exposed when untrusted JSON is parsed from a String, Reader or char[] - for example an HTTP request body already read into a String - rather than from raw UTF-8 bytes.



This issue affects com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-core from 2.16.0 and tools.jackson.core:jackson-core from 3.0.0. Releases before 2.16.0 are not affected, because StreamReadConstraints.maxNameLength was first introduced in jackson-core 2.16.0.

statements.status_notes: This issue is that the maximum property name length is not enforced while jackson-core parses JSON from a String, Reader or char array (UTF-8 byte input is not affected). This copy is Hazelcast's private, relocated Jackson 3 core inside the SonarQube application jar. Hazelcast parses JSON with it only for its HazelcastJsonValue JSON features (JSON metadata indexing and JSON query attribute access) and its Jet JSON helpers, and no SonarQube class references HazelcastJsonValue or Hazelcast Jet. In the single-node configuration of SonarQube Community Build no process starts a Hazelcast member (the launcher creates one only when cluster mode, sonar.cluster.enabled, is set on an application node), so no Hazelcast member exists to receive JSON from another host. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2025-12183
vulnerability.description: Out-of-bounds memory operations in org.lz4:lz4-java 1.8.0 and earlier allow remote attackers to cause denial of service and read adjacent memory via untrusted compressed input.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2025-12183 is an out-of-bounds read in lz4-java's native and unsafe fast decompressors (lz4-java 1.8.0 and earlier): a malformed compressed block makes the decompressor read past the end of its input, which can crash or hang the process and copy adjacent memory into its output. In SonarQube Community Build 26.11 the scanner engine (lib/scanner/sonar-scanner-engine-community-13.16.0.6705.jar) bundles lz4-java 1.4.1; its only user is the Subversion library SVNKit, which the scanner uses when it analyses a project whose working copy contains a .svn directory, or when sonar.scm.provider is svn, to compute blame and, for branch and pull request analysis, changed lines. SVNKit decompresses every delta it receives in svndiff version 2 format with LZ4Factory.fastestInstance().fastDecompressor(), which is the affected decompressor, and a Subversion server that supports it (Subversion 1.10 and later, over svn://) sends deltas in that format by default. The server SVNKit contacts is the one recorded in the working copy that is analysed. A malformed delta from that server can therefore crash or hang the analysis and pull adjacent scanner memory into the analysis. The SonarQube server itself does not run this copy.
statements.action_statement: In SonarQube Community Build 26.11 the scanner engine (lib/scanner/sonar-scanner-engine-community-13.16.0.6705.jar) bundles org.lz4:lz4-java 1.4.1, which is affected when a Subversion project is analysed. The fix is in lz4-java 1.8.1. The scanner engines of SonarQube Server 2026.5.4 and Community Build 26.11 bundle lz4-java 1.4.1, which is also affected, so upgrading SonarQube does not remove the exposure. Analyses run this code when they use the scanner's Subversion support, which the scanner selects when the working copy contains a .svn directory, or when sonar.scm.provider is svn, which a contributor can also set in the repository's sonar-project.properties. For a project that does not use Subversion, set sonar.scm.provider to its real SCM (for example -Dsonar.scm.provider=git) on the scanner command line, which takes precedence over sonar-project.properties. For a Subversion project, setting -Dsonar.scm.disabled=true on the scanner command line removes the exposure, and also turns off blame and changed-line detection. For Subversion projects, use only working copies checked out from your own Subversion server over https.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106452
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.2, net.jpountz.lz4.LZ4BlockInputStream refill() validates that the compressedLen field in a legacy LZ4Block header is nonnegative but allocates a compressed-input buffer of that attacker-controlled size before reading payload data, allowing a header-only stream to request a near-2 GiB allocation and exhaust the JVM heap. Canonical writers emit raw blocks when compression is not smaller than the original block, but vulnerable readers accept non-canonical oversized compressed blocks. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106452 is a heap-exhaustion denial of service in lz4-java's LZ4BlockInputStream.refill(), which allocates a buffer sized by the compressed length field of a block header before reading the payload; it requires an attacker to supply a stream read with LZ4BlockInputStream. In SonarQube Community Build 26.11 the scanner engine (lib/scanner/sonar-scanner-engine-community-13.16.0.6705.jar) bundles lz4-java 1.4.1; its only user is the Subversion library SVNKit, which the scanner uses when it analyses a project whose working copy contains a .svn directory, or when sonar.scm.provider is svn, to compute blame and, for branch and pull request analysis, changed lines. SVNKit calls the LZ4Factory decompressor directly, and classes in the scanner engine outside lz4-java do not reference LZ4BlockInputStream, so an analysis does not run that code. Not exploitable.

vulnerability.name: CVE-2026-106453
vulnerability.description: yawkat LZ4 Java provides LZ4 compression for Java. Prior to 1.11.2, LZ4DecompressorWithLength uses getDecompressedLength to trust the four-byte decompressed-length header before validating the compressed input, allowing a five-byte attacker-supplied input whose header declares a large output size to request up to approximately 2 GiB and exhaust the JVM heap. Convenience overloads backed by LZ4FastDecompressor or LZ4SafeDecompressor allocate the untrusted size, while overloads that write to a caller-provided destination buffer are not affected because the caller controls the destination size. This issue is fixed in version 1.11.2.

statements.status_notes: CVE-2026-106453 is an allocation of up to about 2 GiB in lz4-java's LZ4DecompressorWithLength, driven by the length header of the compressed input. In SonarQube Community Build 26.11 the scanner engine (lib/scanner/sonar-scanner-engine-community-13.16.0.6705.jar) bundles lz4-java 1.4.1, which does not contain the LZ4DecompressorWithLength class; its only user is the Subversion library SVNKit, which the scanner uses when it analyses a project whose working copy contains a .svn directory, or when sonar.scm.provider is svn, to compute blame and, for branch and pull request analysis, changed lines, and it calls the LZ4Factory decompressor directly. Not exploitable.
